ca_west_face_17.blurb: The west-facing side of Daff Dome, a granite dome in the Tuolumne Meadows district of Yosemite National Park. Of the 23 climbs here, most are traditional multipitch lines and a handful are bolted. Difficulty is spread broadly: a few easy options, a solid core of 5.8 to 5.10 cracks and slabs, and a smaller group of 5.11 and 5.12 with one far harder sport line. The stone is solid and varied, with finger cracks, knobby slab, corners and some polished patches, so expect sustained, technical climbing and careful gear placement rather than big power moves. Several lines here are well-known classics of the area.

ca_monkey_to_monk_cliff.blurb: A tall, vertical wall in the Inner Gorge of the Owens River Gorge, reached by walking up through the narrows until the cliff appears ahead. All 23 climbs here are bolted sport routes, running from a couple of 5.8s and a 5.9 up through a big cluster of 5.10 and 5.11, then a healthy group of 5.12 and two 5.13s. Pitches run roughly 90 to 120 feet. It suits climbers who like sustained vertical face climbing in a canyon setting, and the 5.10 to 5.12 range is where most of the choice lies.

ca_owl_tor.blurb: A steep, strongly overhanging crag in the hills east of Santa Maria on the Central Coast. All 23 routes are bolted sport lines on pocketed, powerful terrain, with a single route in the 5.11 range, plenty of 5.12 and 5.13, and a few at 5.14. It is a place for strong, power-endurance climbers rather than anyone building up; there is very little here for easier grades. Expect wet pockets and seepage after a heavy rain season, and let it dry out before you go.

ca_chiquito_dome.blurb: A large south-facing dome of roughly 500 feet on Shuteye Ridge in the Sierra Nevada foothills, a quieter alternative to the busier Yosemite crags. The 23 listed climbs split between bolted sport lines and traditional routes, many of them multipitch, from 5.7 up to 5.13 with the heart of the range around 5.9 to 5.12. The right side is slabbier and gentler, while the left is steeper with the longer, harder lines. Faces are knobby and slabby with small flakes and thin cracks. Bring plenty of quickdraws and a long rope, and carry extra water in warm weather.

ca_main_wall_7.blurb: The principal face of Hawk Dome, a well-featured granite dome near Fresno Dome in the Sierra National Forest above Bass Lake. The wall holds 23 routes, a little over half traditional and the rest bolted, most of them one to three pitches. Grades run from 5.7 to 5.11, with the largest share around 5.10 and a good handful of easier 5.7 to 5.9 lines, so it suits intermediate leaders. Reaching it takes a short hike on well-marked trails through pine forest; watch for loose rock near the base.

ca_east_face_2.blurb: The east side of the Monolith, a large freestanding block on the canyon floor in the eastern part of Pinnacles National Park. It is mostly a sport face with a few traditional lines, one aid line and one top-rope. Of 23 climbs, the bulk fall at 5.11 and 5.12, with a handful of easier 5.5 to 5.8 options and a couple of 5.13 and 5.14 test pieces. The rock is steep, solid and highly featured, making it one of the park's most popular walls.

ca_lower_buttress.blurb: A large granite slab of about 350 feet at Lover's Leap near Strawberry, west of South Lake Tahoe. Of 23 climbs here, nearly all are traditional multipitch routes with a few bolted lines. The face is crossed by plentiful horizontal dikes, with terrain from slightly overhanging to slightly slabby, cracks and knobs. Grades start at easy 5.5 and 5.7 classics, centre on 5.10 and 5.11, and top out with a few 5.12s. It works well for a day of moderate multipitch, and it is one of the easier faces at the Leap to reach.
